The Deepwater flathead (Platycephalus conatus) is a bottom-dwelling percomorph found on the continental shelf of temperate Australian waters. Newly hatched larvae are minute, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of about 0.5 millimeters. At a water temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C], the age at birth reaches approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days], a brief incubation period consistent with the small, pelagic eggs typical of this family.

Juvenile Deepwater flathead grow steadily on the sandy and muddy substrates of the continental shelf, feeding on small benthic invertebrates and fishes while relying on cryptic coloration for concealment from predators. Individuals reach the total length at puberty of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters], a size that marks the onset of gonadal maturation after several years of sustained growth on the shelf.

Adults of this species ultimately attain a substantial total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 2,134 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,134 grams]. This considerable adult body size, among the largest of the flatheads found in Australian waters, supports the species' ecological role as an ambush predator on the continental shelf, where its dorsoventrally flattened body plan allows it to lie concealed on the seabed while awaiting passing prey.

Longevity in the Deepwater flathead reaches a maximum of approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] at the same reference temperature of 14.4 °C [T = 14.4 °C], a considerable lifespan for a demersal percomorph of this size. This extended longevity, combined with delayed maturation at 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters], is consistent with a moderately slow life-history strategy typical of continental shelf fishes that experience relatively stable environmental conditions and comparatively low natural mortality once they reach adult size.
